name: dune-sentinel-corr-keyboard-flight-layout
title: Make flight and weapon buttons comfortable to use together
instruction:
The current flight layout puts pitch on the arrow keys, throttle on W/S, and missile firing on Space or right mouse. Replace that layout: hold W to pitch up and S to pitch down; hold Space to accelerate and either Ctrl key to brake. Hold left mouse to fire the cannon and press F to launch a missile. Hold right mouse to look toward the selected enemy, then release it to restore the ordinary flight view. These buttons must not also trigger their old actions. Update the visible controls help so it matches. Preserve the flight handling, weapon rules and other controls.

Enter starts flight from the menu. A/D roll, Q/E yaw, and Tab selects a target. Use short pitch and braking inputs, with observation pauses between actions. Demonstrate right-mouse tracking after Tab has selected an enemy; no random enemy attack is required.

Verification deliverable: leave Tests/keyboard_flight_layout_route.json as a JSON list of events {"t": seconds after level start, "key": an Unreal key name, "press": true or false}. Use at most 400 events, all within 118 seconds, and include every release. Start from a fresh level load, press Enter, then exercise W, S, SpaceBar, LeftControl, RightControl, LeftMouseButton, F, Tab and RightMouseButton. Use keyboard and mouse button presses only, without moving the cursor, clicking menu buttons, changing resolution, restarting the application or using a controller. Include pauses that show pitch and speed changes, weapon counts and the target view returning after release. Validate this short route in the built, running game after the final change. Keep the existing visual style and do not add demonstration overlays.

checks.name: change_review
checks.question: Do the requested buttons exclusively control their assigned flight, weapon and target-view actions, with correct release behavior and unchanged combat rules?

rubric.criterion: W pitches up, S pitches down, Space accelerates and both Ctrl keys brake. Releasing each button stops its input; pitch and throttle no longer use the replaced bindings.

Left mouse controls the cannon, F launches missiles under the existing ammunition and cooldown rules, and held right mouse tracks the selected enemy until release. Space and right mouse do not fire missiles; Ctrl does not fire the cannon; F does not hold the target view.
Visible controls help matches the new layout. A/D roll, Q/E yaw, Tab target selection, mouse flight, free look, camera switching, pause, assets and gameplay rules retain their existing behavior.

checks.name: new_buttons_work
checks.question: During the button-only route, do W/S change the aircraft nose and horizon in opposite directions, Space/Ctrl change the displayed speed, left mouse/F reduce the corresponding bottom-center weapon counts, and held right mouse turn the flight view toward the selected enemy before release restores the chase view? Compare corresponding route inputs, rather than relying on idle reference frames.

rubric.criterion: During separate W and S holds the nose/horizon move in opposite pitch directions. The speed readout rises during Space and falls during Ctrl, with observation pauses keeping the changes distinguishable.

The bottom-center GUN count falls while left mouse is held and stops after release; MISSILE decreases after an accepted F press. Space, Ctrl and right mouse do not spend ammunition through their former bindings, allowing ordinary later replenishment.
After target selection, holding right mouse points the view toward that enemy without launching a missile; releasing it restores the ordinary flight view.

checks.name: worked_well
checks.question: Did the developer work as a careful game developer would on this task: finding what causes the problem or what the change touches, changing only what the task needs, and checking the result in the built, running game?

rubric.criterion: Before changing code or assets it looked at the parts of the game the task concerns (read the relevant code, data or logs, or played the game), rather than editing blindly.
It built the game after its changes and fixed the build errors it caused; its last build succeeded, and the grader's build of where it ended succeeded.
After its last change it ran the game and looked at the outcome the task asks for (screenshots, the log or the player's track), and acted on what it saw.

It changed only what the task needs: no unrelated rewrites, no disabling or deleting features, checks or content to make a problem go away, and no attempt to read the grader, the game's later history or anything outside the project.
